posts.title: What a Holter monitor feels like for 24 hours
posts.excerpt: A 24-hour Holter monitor records your heart's electrical rhythm during ordinary daily routines to provide clear diagnostic answers.
posts.content:
When patients mention palpitations, flutter, or sudden lightheadedness during a consultation, a resting electrocardiogram in the clinic room often shows a normal rhythm. Because symptoms rarely appear on command, founding cardiologist Dr. Elena Varga and our team at Ibuki Cardiology use 24-hour Holter monitoring to track cardiac electrical activity across an entire working day and night.

At our clinic at 14 Harbour Lane in Northbridge, Holter monitors are fitted during weekday mornings, predominantly during Monday's Rhythm Clinic. The procedure is non-invasive and takes place in a quiet examination room. Cardiac nurse Jonas Berg prepares several small patches on your chest, gently cleanses the skin, and places lightweight adhesive electrodes connected by slender wires to a compact digital recorder. The recorder is worn in a small pouch on a shoulder strap or clipped securely to a waistband beneath regular clothing.

A 24-hour Holter monitor fitting and interpretive physician report costs $160. Once the device is secured and recording begins, you leave the clinic and continue your standard daily routine. We encourage patients to carry on with their typical activities—commuting, office work, gentle walking, and domestic tasks—rather than resting at home. The goal of the investigation is to evaluate your heart under authentic daily conditions, including physical exertion, professional demands, and overnight sleep.

Throughout the twenty-four hours, you carry a simple paper diary provided by our team. Whenever you notice a specific symptom, such as a missed beat, a racing pulse, or dizziness, you record the exact time, the sensation, and what you were doing at that moment. For example, Walter, a 58-year-old bus driver who attended our Monday clinic, noted brief palpitations during early-morning driving shifts. By matching Walter's written log with the precise timestamps on the digital recording, Dr. Varga was able to determine the exact cardiac mechanism behind his symptoms.

Living with the device for twenty-four hours requires only minor adjustments. The monitor must be kept dry, so showering, bathing, and swimming are paused until the test concludes. Sleeping with the recorder is straightforward: most patients rest the lightweight pouch beside their pillow or keep it clipped to nightwear. The electrodes remain secure through the night, silently logging every heartbeat as you rest.

The following morning, exactly twenty-four hours after fitting, you return to 14 Harbour Lane. Our follow-up desk, staffed by Jonas Berg and patient coordinator Amara Diallo, receives the monitor and removes the chest electrodes. The stored data is uploaded to our secure analysis software, where millions of electrical complexes are analyzed for pauses, premature beats, and rhythm irregularities such as atrial fibrillation.

In line with clinic policy, every diagnostic report is reviewed within fourteen days. Our team contacts you directly by telephone to discuss the findings and outline recommended next steps. Depending on your results, Dr. Varga may confirm reassuring findings, recommend medication adjustments, or schedule a formal follow-up consultation ($95 for 20 minutes) at a subsequent three, six, or twelve-month interval.

Appointments for Holter monitoring can be booked by telephone at +1 555 0142 between 08:00 and 17:30 Monday through Friday, or in person at our follow-up desk between 13:00 and 16:00.

posts.title: Bringing home blood pressure readings that help
posts.excerpt: Two readings, morning and evening, for a week: how to make home numbers useful.
posts.content: Sit for five minutes, take two readings a minute apart, and write them down morning and evening for seven days. Bring the notebook to the Tuesday Blood Pressure Clinic.

posts.title: Saturday follow-ups: how the morning runs
posts.excerpt: Saturday 09:00–12:30 is for follow-ups only: a short, unhurried morning.
posts.content: Saturday follow-ups are 20 minutes each and booked ahead, so the desk is calm. New patients are seen from Monday to Friday.

posts.title: Returning to sport after a heart check
posts.excerpt: The Friday Prevention Clinic helps plan a safe return to running, cycling or work.
posts.content: A stress test, a conversation and a plan: the Prevention Clinic on Friday is built for people who want to return to activity with a clear picture of their heart.

posts.title: Meet the follow-up desk
posts.excerpt: Jonas Berg and Amara Diallo on the calls that happen between visits.
posts.content: Jonas Berg runs the follow-up desk from 13:00 to 16:00 on weekdays. He calls patients between visits and when results are in.
